parts.title: The Science and Importance of Sunscreen
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Many people enjoy sunny days at the beach, in the park or on the football field, but the same sunlight that lifts our mood can also damage our skin. Too much ultraviolet light, or UV, can cause painful burns and may lead to skin cancer over many years. For this reason, sunscreen is a **vital** part of staying safe outdoors. Millions of people use it every summer, yet many still make simple mistakes. This passage explains how it works and how to use it well.

Sunlight contains two main types of UV that reach the ground, called UVA and UVB. UVB is the main cause of sunburn, while UVA goes deeper into the skin and is reportedly linked to ageing and to DNA damage that may increase the risk of melanoma. The number on a bottle, called the sun protection factor or SPF, mainly measures protection against UVB. As a rough guide, SPF 15 blocks about 93 per cent of burning rays, SPF 30 about 97 per cent and SPF 50 about 98 per cent. A higher number therefore gives only a small extra benefit, and it does not last longer. The SPF rating itself was reportedly introduced by Franz Greiter in 1974.

There are two main kinds of sunscreen, and they work in different ways. Mineral sunscreens contain zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, which sit on top of the skin and mainly absorb UV, although they also **reflect** and scatter some of it. Chemical sunscreens absorb UV and release the energy as heat, and many people find these products lighter and easier to rub in. Mineral products are often preferred by people with sensitive skin, although they can leave a pale film. Some chemicals have caused concern for the oceans, and Hawaii banned sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate in 2018 to protect its coral reefs.

Using sunscreen correctly matters as much as choosing a good one in the first place. An average adult needs about 35 millilitres, or roughly six teaspoons, to cover the whole body, but studies suggest that people usually apply only a quarter to a half of that amount. Look for a broad-spectrum product, which protects against both UVA and UVB, and reapply it every two hours. Parents should take extra care with their children, and it is wise to protect **them** with shade, hats and sunscreen.

Sunscreen is not magic, and it works best together with other habits. Staying in the shade at midday, wearing a hat and light clothing, and avoiding long periods in strong sun all reduce the amount of UV reaching the skin. Some people worry that sunscreen reduces vitamin D, but typical use usually does not cause a deficiency, and fatty fish and supplements are other sources. In short, a few minutes of care before going outside can protect the skin for life.

parts.title: Electronic Waste and Its Toxic Legacy in Tiger Shark Populations
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: The world now produces a **staggering** quantity of electronic waste, with an estimated 62 million tonnes generated in 2022, reportedly 82 per cent more than in 2010. Forecasts suggest that the figure could reach 82 million tonnes by 2030. Only about 22 per cent of the total was formally collected and recycled, so much of the rest may end up in landfill, in storage or in informal recycling. This growing pile is more than an inconvenience, because many of its components are poisonous.

Electronic devices contain lead, mercury, cadmium and brominated flame retardants, substances that are harmless while sealed inside a working phone but dangerous once casings are crushed or burned. E-waste reportedly makes up about three per cent of landfill waste but around 70 per cent of its toxic material. When rain washes leaked metals and chemicals from dumps into rivers, they can eventually travel to the sea. Once there, persistent compounds can enter the food chain, where concentrations tend to increase at each step.

Few animals illustrate this problem better than the tiger shark, a large tropical predator. Adults typically measure between three and a half and almost five metres, and the species has the widest diet of any shark, eating fish, seabirds, turtles, rays and even other sharks. Its habit of swallowing almost anything has earned it the nickname garbage can of the sea, and licence plates and tyres have reportedly been found in stomachs. As an apex predator, it sits at the top of the food chain and may collect contaminants carried by everything beneath it.

Researchers have reportedly detected flame retardants and heavy metals in several shark species, although direct evidence linking tiger shark decline to electronic waste remains limited. Their biology nevertheless makes the problem plausible, since tiger sharks reportedly live beyond twelve years, mature slowly and carry pups for up to sixteen months. Females mate only about once every three years, so any harm to reproduction could leave a population in a **precarious** position for decades. The species is already listed as near threatened, mainly because of fishing and finning.

The same dumps that may threaten marine life also endanger the people who work in them. Informal recycling sites rely on workers, many of **whom** handle toxic materials with little protective equipment. At Agbogbloshie in Ghana, soil samples reportedly contained lead at up to 18,125 parts per million, far above the 400 considered acceptable for play areas by the United States environmental agency. In Guiyu in China, a study found that children's average blood lead level was 15.3 micrograms per decilitre, compared with 9.9 at a control site.

Solving the problem requires action at several levels, beginning with the design of devices that last longer, contain fewer hazardous substances and can be repaired or recycled easily. The Basel Convention of 1989 regulates the movement of hazardous waste between countries, and the European Union has reportedly restricted lead, mercury and cadmium in new products since 2003. Consumers can help by keeping devices longer and returning old ones to certified collectors. Whether such measures arrive in time to protect long-lived predators such as the tiger shark remains uncertain, but the evidence for action is already strong.

parts.title: Hanoi Cuisine: Identity, Heritage, and the Pressures of Modernity
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Few cities define themselves through food as completely as Hanoi, where a bowl of noodles can carry as much meaning as a monument. Dishes such as phở, bún chả and chả cá Lã Vọng are celebrated far beyond Vietnam, yet their northern roots and careful rules are often overlooked by international diners. This passage examines how the cuisine expresses identity and how it is changing. The story is one of heritage, adaptation and anxiety about what may be lost.

Northern cooking is often described as the most **austere** of Vietnam's three regional traditions, because it relies on subtle combinations of ingredients rather than strong sweet, sour or spicy notes. Colder weather reportedly limited the use of spices, so black pepper rather than chilli became the main source of heat. Freshwater fish, crabs and shellfish feature prominently, and dill may garnish fish dishes. The result is a cuisine that rewards attention rather than demanding it.

Behind this restraint lies a philosophy of balance, in which the five tastes of spicy, sour, bitter, salty and sweet are each linked to an element and an organ. Dishes also aim to combine several colours, and ingredients are judged as warming or cooling according to yin and yang. Duck, regarded as a cooling meat, is traditionally paired with warming ginger fish sauce. Fish sauce itself, made from fermented raw fish, appears on almost every table.

Colonial history added another layer, because French rule reportedly made beef more widely eaten, introduced produce such as potatoes, tomatoes and carrots, and inspired dishes like bò sốt vang. The baguette became bánh mì, which is now one of the country's most popular fast foods. Such borrowings were absorbed on local terms, with Vietnamese cooks adapting foreign ingredients to existing principles of balance instead of copying French recipes.

Phở, perhaps the best known export of northern cooking, is said to have originated in Van Cu in Nam Định province, and it later developed distinct northern, Huế and Saigon styles. Other northern dishes, including bún riêu and bánh cuốn, spread southwards with migration. Recognition abroad has followed, and CNN reportedly included phở in a 2024 list of the world's best soups, while Vietnam has held an annual Phở Day since 2017.

Modernity brings opportunity to the kitchens of the capital, but it also brings pressure. **[1]** Tourism has widened the audience, and visitors now queue at stalls that once served mainly neighbours and office workers. **[2]** Authorities in several Asian cities have reportedly tried to move street vendors off the pavements, a policy that many residents regard as a threat to everyday food culture. **[3]** In some kitchens, artificial food dyes are reportedly replacing traditional natural colourings, a quiet substitution that few diners notice. **[4]** That erosion would be hard to reverse, because flavour memory passes from household to household through meals rather than through books.

Preserving a food culture is therefore not simply a matter of freezing recipes in time, because dishes live through the daily choices of cooks and customers. Some younger chefs reportedly reinterpret classic dishes rather than abandon **them**, adjusting portions and presentation while keeping the underlying balance. Efforts to **codify** authentic recipes may help to protect heritage, yet they risk turning a living tradition into a museum piece. In Hanoi, as elsewhere, identity is kept alive by eating, not merely by remembering.

parts.title: Agarwood and Aquilaria crassna: Biology, Trade, and the Limits of Conservation
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Few natural products are as **coveted** as agarwood, the dark, fragrant resinous heartwood that forms inside certain trees and is burned as incense or distilled into the perfume ingredient known as oud. Its value is so high that it is counted among the world's most expensive woods. One of its commonly harvested sources, Aquilaria crassna, is native to Southeast Asia. This passage examines how the resin forms, why trade in it is so lucrative, and whether conservation can keep pace.

Agarwood is not a normal part of a healthy tree, but a response to injury, because an ambrosia beetle bores into the trunk or roots and a mould, Phaeoacremonium parasitica, then infects the wound. The tree defends itself by producing resin, and the heartwood darkens and becomes denser, shifting from pale beige to red, brown or even black. In natural forests, only about seven in a hundred trees reportedly become infected. Rarity at the source therefore sets the scarcity that drives the market.

The genus Aquilaria contains about seventeen species, of which nine are known to produce agarwood, and Aquilaria malaccensis has long been regarded as the primary source. Aquilaria crassna and Aquilaria sinensis are also commonly harvested, and several species occur in Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. Because only a small share of wild trees contains resin, harvesters may fell many in the hope of finding it, a practice that quickly thins the forest.

Superior pure agarwood has reportedly sold for as much as US$290,000 per kilogram, while adulterated or plantation material can fetch as little as US$100, a disparity of almost three thousand times. **[1]** That incentive is far from new, since Indian texts reportedly describe agarwood as a fragrant product as early as 1400 BCE. **[2]** Egyptian funeral rites reportedly used it more than three thousand years ago. **[3]** Modern demand centres on perfumery, where oud is a common base note, often paired with rose, and on incense used in religious and domestic settings. [4] The oil is chemically complex, and about 70 kilograms of wood yield no more than 20 millilitres.

International regulation has tried to slow this exploitation, and CITES listed Aquilaria malaccensis in Appendix II in 1995 before extending the listing to every Aquilaria species in 2004. Aquilaria crassna, **whose** wild populations have shrunk under harvesting pressure, is assessed as critically endangered by the IUCN. Listing in Appendix II does not ban trade, however, but requires exports to be licensed and shown not to damage wild populations, which depends on honest monitoring by exporting countries.

Plantations offer an apparent solution, since trees can be inoculated with fungus to induce resin, and commercial plantations reportedly exist in India, Bangladesh and Bhutan. Yet inoculation techniques have varied in effectiveness, and some buyers dismiss the plantation product as fake. The profits at stake have long been large, since a pound of Calambac bought in Hội An for 15 taels could reportedly be sold in Nagasaki for 600 taels. Meanwhile, the premium paid for wild resin sustains a **clandestine** trade that may keep drawing harvesters into protected forests.

Conservation of agarwood therefore faces a structural problem, because the very scarcity that protects the resin's value also pays for its destruction in remote forests. Licensing, plantations and monitoring each help, yet none removes the incentive to harvest wild trees while prices remain so high. A more durable answer may lie in making cultivated resin trusted and affordable enough to compete with the wild product. Until that happens, the trees themselves will continue to pay the price.

3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):
• Luôn so sánh các phương án thay vì phân tích riêng lẻ.
• Dùng hiện tại đơn để mô tả sở thích và điều kiện giả định khi đánh giá lựa chọn.

• Compared to – so với
• Moreover – hơn nữa
• Therefore – vì vậy

6. Tư duy làm bài nói:

• Sử dụng cấu trúc IDEA: Introduction – Detail – Example – Add.

• Ví dụ 2: In addition, technology can help people improve their communication and teamwork skills.
• Giải thích từng kỹ năng bằng ví dụ thực tế.
• Bám sát sơ đồ tư duy để tránh lạc đề.
3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):
• Dùng các câu chuyển ý mượt mà giữa các nhánh.

Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:
• time management – quản lý thời gian

• Furthermore – hơn nữa
• In conclusion – kết luận
